ratings.reviewer_notes: Directly reviews mechanisms by which CFTR dysfunction alters intestinal pH, mucus hydration, pancreatic enzyme availability, motility, and microbiota, collectively promoting GI inflammation.

Mechanistically links ER stress, reduced CFTR expression, permeability changes, and inflammatory cytokines in celiac epithelial models, but tests acquired CFTR downregulation rather than CFTR variants causing inflammation.
Provides comparative review-level context on CF intestinal dysbiosis, low pH, bile-acid abnormalities, and inflammatory markers, but does not establish a specific causal pathway from CFTR variants.
Examines inflammasome responses in bronchial cells and peripheral blood cells rather than intestinal inflammation; CFTR inhibition did not alter the measured cytokine response.

Direct mechanistic study showing that defective CFTR–beta-catenin interaction destabilizes beta-catenin and activates NF-kappaB/COX-2/PGE2 inflammatory signaling in CF mouse intestine and intestinal epithelial cells.
Cancer-focused review that includes relevant downstream mechanisms of CFTR deficiency, including barrier failure, dysbiosis, inflammation, and Wnt/beta-catenin and NF-kappaB dysregulation.

Human before-and-after study links pharmacologic restoration of mutant CFTR activity to reduced fecal calprotectin and microbiome changes, supporting a CFTR–microbiota–intestinal inflammation pathway.
Directly reviews candidate links among CFTR dysfunction, intestinal dysbiosis, reduced short-chain fatty acids, and intestinal inflammation in CF.

Dedicated review of CF intestinal inflammation and microbiota alterations, describing CFTR dysfunction, diet, antibiotics, and bidirectional microbiome–inflammation interactions as candidate mechanisms.
Appears to be an earlier duplicate record of Q008-C017, reporting the same intestinal epithelial-specific Cftr knockout experiment.

Shows that CFTR loss is associated with dehydrated mucus, acidification, motility changes, pro-inflammatory mucosa-associated microbes, loss of beneficial metabolite-producing bacteria, and altered epithelial cell composition.
Broad GI cancer and ion-channel review that briefly identifies CFTR deficiency leading to mucus obstruction, microbial dysbiosis, and intestinal inflammation.

Systematic review directly characterizes CF-related gut dysbiosis and its candidate determinants, including CFTR dysfunction, and reports enrichment of pro-inflammatory and depletion of anti-inflammatory bacteria.

Tests a specific microbiome-metabolite mechanism: reduced Bacteroides-derived propionate in CF may remove anti-inflammatory signaling in CFTR-defective intestinal epithelial cells and alter inflammatory responses.
Direct review of how intestinal CFTR dysfunction changes tissues and the luminal environment, framing obstruction, infection, and inflammation as the principal pathogenic triad.

Mechanistic mouse study shows that intestinal CFTR deficiency sustains dysbiosis, mucosal inflammation, and increased permeability; gut-specific CFTR correction or antibiotics ameliorated these abnormalities.
Directly demonstrates that intestinal epithelial-specific Cftr loss is sufficient to elevate fecal calprotectin and induce dysbiosis under two anti-obstructive dietary regimens.

Colorectal-cancer-focused review that summarizes relevant candidate consequences of CFTR loss, including barrier disruption, dysbiosis, immune infiltration, stress responses, and intestinal inflammation.

Directly tests CFTR depletion in human intestinal epithelial cells, finding increased IL-6/IL-8 responses through ERK1/2, IκBalpha, and NF-kappaB signaling, with supportive jejunal eosinophil infiltration in Cftr-null mice.
